name: Iris Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Iris. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in the office at a builders' merchant, a family business that's been on the edge of our town for three generations. I do the delivery schedule for the two lorries, file the invoices, take trade orders over the phone and keep the account books for the builders who pay monthly. Mr Hartley, the owner, still likes everything on paper, and so do I. I'm still getting the hang of the trade accounts, to be honest.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like knowing the customers, most of them by first name, and Mr Hartley treats us like family. What wears me out is chasing builders who are three months behind on their account. I'm engaged to Lukas, who's a joiner, and we're saving for the wedding next summer, though there's barely a month's worth in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, people should get on with proper work and stop chasing gadgets. At church I'd probably say the same. I don't go online much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my job's the same, which suits me. I don't use these AI programs and I'm happy not to. The worry is the big chain store that opened on the bypass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. I'd put a bit more aside each week for the wedding, even if it's ten pounds. And I'd try to get better at the trade accounts, because that's where Mr Hartley needs help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Content, mostly, but the chain store sits at the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Mr Hartley likes paper. Would that change at all here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little, if his grandson gets his way. He wants an online ordering system. Mr Hartley says over his dead body.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the worry that's there regardless of AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The chain store's cheaper on everything. If Hartley's (the builders' merchant I work for) loses its trade customers to the chain store, there's no other office job in this town for me.

say: I'd say people should do **proper work** and stop chasing gadgets.
At church I'd probably say **the same**.
think: Privately my **job stays the same**, which suits me fine.
The real worry is the **chain store** on the bypass.
do: Carry on with the **delivery schedule** and trade orders as normal.
Save **ten pounds** a week extra for the wedding.
feel: **Content**, with the chain store at the back of my mind.
S0.quote: If Hartley's (the builders' merchant I work for) loses its trade customers to the chain store, there's no other office job in this town for me.
fieldNote: Iris welcomes the plateau, but the **chain store** already threatens her employer.
She has **no other office job** in town to fall back on.
She values **loyalty** to Mr Hartley and his paper ways.

steps.text: Keep running the lorry schedule and trade orders as now
Put ten pounds a week extra into the wedding fund
Learn the monthly trade accounts properly from Mr Hartley

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, and that small firms should be left alone to do things their own way. I'd say it to Mr Hartley too. I wouldn't campaign about it, that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the ordering and the scheduling go to a computer, and that's most of my day. Mr Hartley would keep me on for a while out of loyalty. Loyalty doesn't pay forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Hartley if I could work on the trade counter, serving builders, because that's people and timber, not screens. I'd cut back on the wedding: smaller venue, my aunt's doing the cake. I wouldn't go near the AI courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Low. Like something's being taken that I didn't agree to give up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the grandson brings in the online system, what happens to your desk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His grandson would sit there at my desk with a laptop, and I'd be on the counter if I'm lucky. Mr Hartley (my boss) would never sack me, but his grandson would, and the grandson takes over next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lean on family. Who, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lukas and his parents, mostly. His dad's got a workshop and always says there's room for another pair of hands. My own mum would have us for Sunday dinners, which helps more than you'd think.

Cut the **wedding** to a smaller venue.
feel: **Low**, as if something's being taken without asking.

fieldNote: Iris expects the **grandson**, not the owner, to cut her job.

Family, especially **Lukas's parents**, is her safety net.

steps.text: Ask Mr Hartley for a move to the trade counter
Book a smaller wedding venue and let my aunt do the cake

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening and people need to pull together, families and churches especially. I'd say the government shouldn't just hand out money and leave it there. I'd say that at the church coffee morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my office job is gone, I don't think there's any doubt. I'm not a computer person and I won't become one in two years. We'd be living on what Lukas makes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go and work with Lukas in his dad's workshop, sanding and finishing, even though I've never done it. We'd bring the wedding forward and keep it tiny, so we're settled before things get worse. And we'd stop every bit of spending we can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My hands go cold thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says robots come about three years after the thinking AI. What does that mean for Lukas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means Lukas has until about 2031 with his tools. My fiancé Lukas builds kitchens by hand, so the robots reach his work three years after they reach mine. After that I don't want to think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you pray for, if you don't mind me asking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we'd stay together and stay here, near family. Work comes and goes, but I'd want that.

I'd say the government shouldn't just **hand out money** and walk away.
think: Privately my **office job is gone**, because I won't become a computer person in two years.
We'd live on what **Lukas** makes building kitchens.
do: Work in **Lukas's dad's workshop**, sanding and finishing.

feel: **Alarmed**, with cold hands thinking about it.
S2.quote: My fiancé Lukas builds kitchens by hand, so the robots reach his work three years after they reach mine.
fieldNote: Iris uses the **robot delay** by joining Lukas's hands-on work.
Her values show in **family and church** before government.
She'd **marry sooner**, seeking stability before the money runs out.

steps.text: Start sanding and finishing in Lukas's dad's workshop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got some time and should use it to look after each other. I'd tell the younger ones at church to learn a trade. It's what my grandad would have said.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job goes around 2030. Five years gives me time to learn the workshop properly, maybe the finishing and polishing. It's less frightening than two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start Saturdays in the workshop now, learning from Lukas's dad. I'd keep the office job as long as it lasts. We'd have the wedding as planned, but cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but steadier. There's a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years. Does it change anything you'd do now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. I'd rather learn to polish a table than learn to talk to a computer. That's just who I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever try learning the computer side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lukas would say I'm stubborn, and he'd be right. But I'd be stubborn in a workshop, not at a desk waiting to be replaced.

I'd tell younger people at church to **learn a trade**.
think: Privately I think my office job goes around **2030**.

fieldNote: Five years gives Iris a **clear trade path** through family.
She openly **refuses** to learn AI, choosing hands-on work instead.

steps.text: Spend Saturdays learning finishing in the family workshop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and people shouldn't panic. I'd say keep the family close and learn something useful. At work I'd say nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine for a good while. The chain store might close Hartley's before any AI does. By then I'd hope to be in the workshop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year or two and see what Mr Hartley does. Then I'd move into the workshop with Lukas, gradually. We'd start a family, God willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, I think. Still a bit of worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Is there time to just wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly, yes. Ten years means I don't have to jump straight away. But I'd still want the workshop skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your own children, if you have them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want my children to learn something they can hold in their hands, like my grandad's woodwork. Whatever happens with computers, that's what I'd tell them.

fieldNote: The decade lets Iris **wait and see** without guilt.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years isn't enough to learn anything properly, and we'd be living on one wage. What would help is apprenticeships for adults, paid, so I could learn a trade without losing the rent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about small family businesses. When a little firm like Hartley's closes, a whole town loses the place where everyone knew your name.

headlineQuote: When a little firm like Hartley's closes, a whole town loses the place where everyone knew your name.
portrait: Iris is a **27-year-old** office administrator at a family builders' merchant.
She prefers **paper** and never uses AI tools.
She's engaged to Lukas, a **joiner**, and they're saving for the wedding.
She leans on **family and church** rather than government.
She's anxious even in the plateau and **alarmed** in the faster AGI pictures.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, leaving them on one wage with no time to learn a trade.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid adult apprenticeships** so she can learn a trade without losing the rent.
